content: Hysterectomy performed via an abdominal approach can involve the removal of either the uterus alone, referred to as a subtotal hysterectomy (STH), or the removal of both the uterus and the cervix, known as a total hysterectomy (TH). Total hysterectomy is the more commonly performed procedure, but the outcomes of these two surgical approaches have not been systematically compared. The objective of this study was to evaluate and compare the short-term and long-term outcomes of subtotal hysterectomy versus total hysterectomy in the treatment of benign gynecological conditions. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Menstrual Disorders and Subfertility Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, and others, covering studies published up to July 2011. Only randomized controlled trials involving women undergoing either STH or TH for benign gynecological conditions were included in the analysis. A total of nine trials, encompassing 1,553 participants, were included in the review. The trials were independently selected, assessed for risk of bias, and analyzed by two reviewers, with their findings compared to ensure accuracy. The results revealed no significant differences between STH and TH in terms of urinary, bowel, or sexual function outcomes, both in the short term (up to two years post-surgery) and the long term (up to nine years post-surgery). However, the duration of the surgical procedure was shorter by approximately 11 minutes, and the volume of blood loss during surgery was reduced by an average of 57 milliliters in the STH group compared to the TH group. Despite these differences, they were not considered to provide a meaningful clinical advantage, and there was no significant difference in the likelihood of requiring a blood transfusion between the two groups. Postoperative complications showed some variation. Women undergoing STH were less likely to experience postoperative fever (odds ratio [OR] 0.48, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.3 to 0.8) and urinary retention (OR 0.23, 95% CI 0.1 to 0.8) compared to those undergoing TH. However, women in the STH group were significantly more likely to experience ongoing cyclical vaginal bleeding up to two years after surgery (OR 16.0, 95% CI 6.1 to 41.6). There were no significant differences between the two procedures in terms of other complications, recovery time, resolution of preoperative symptoms, or hospital readmission rates. It is worth noting that trials comparing laparoscopic approaches were underpowered to detect certain differences. In conclusion, this review does not support the notion that subtotal hysterectomy provides superior outcomes in terms of sexual, urinary, or bowel function compared to total abdominal hysterectomy. However, women undergoing subtotal hysterectomy are more likely to experience ongoing cyclical bleeding for up to a year post-surgery compared to those undergoing total hysterectomy.
